exam: A patient presents with unilateral tongue deviation and dysphagia after carotid endarterectomy — discuss the likely nerve injured and immediate management — identify hypoglossal nerve injury; secure airway, assess for bilateral involvement, arrange imaging.
During a neurological exam you note tongue atrophy but normal palate elevation — what does this localise to and why? — Isolated hypoglossal lesion; palate supplied by CN X.

A 45‑year‑old with tuberculous meningitis develops tongue fasciculations — which cranial nerve is affected and what is the pathophysiology? — CN XII involvement due to basal meningitis compressing the nerve.

How would you differentiate a central (cortical) speech disorder from a peripheral hypoglossal palsy at the bedside? — Central lesions spare tongue deviation; peripheral shows deviation toward weak side.
In a low‑resource setting you suspect hypoglossal nerve compression by a neck tumour but lack MRI — what alternative investigations can you use? — CT neck, bedside ultrasound, clinical localisation.
What are the emergency priorities for bilateral hypoglossal palsy? — Protect airway, consider intubation, monitor for aspiration, treat underlying cause.
Why is a lingual artery injury a concern during hypoglossal nerve surgery? — The artery runs alongside the nerve; injury can cause tongue hematoma and airway obstruction.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy presents with tongue weakness — list tropical infections that can affect CN XII and the rationale for each. — TB meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, syphilis; all can cause basal meningitis compressing the nerve.
ai.title: Hypoglossal Nerve Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies motor fibers to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, enabling speech, swallowing and airway patency. Its course from the medulla to the tongue makes it vulnerable to lesions at the skull base, neck, and oral cavity.

b: Motor to tongue → speech, chewing, swallowing
sections.p: The hypoglossal nerve is a purely motor cranial nerve that originates from the hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla and exits the skull through the hypoglossal canal.

b: Runs lateral to the internal carotid artery in the carotid sheath
Crosses the hyoglossus muscle before entering the tongue
sections.p: After leaving the medulla, the nerve descends between the vertebral artery and the anterior spinal artery, passes through the hypoglossal canal, and travels deep to the posterior belly of the digastric before turning anteriorly to the tongue.

b: Close to the lingual artery (branch of external carotid)
Adjacent to the ansa cervicalis loop
sections.p: In the neck, the hypoglossal nerve lies superficial to the internal jugular vein and deep to the posterior belly of the digastric, making it susceptible during carotid endarterectomy and neck dissection.
Arterial supply follows the lingual artery, a branch of the external carotid, which runs alongside the nerve in the submandibular region.

b: Proprioceptive fibers travel with V3 to the mesencephalic nucleus
sections.p: The hypoglossal nerve receives no parasympathetic fibers; it is purely somatic motor. It receives proprioceptive feedback via the trigeminal nerve (V) for tongue position.

Activation of the intrinsic tongue muscles changes tongue shape for articulation, while extrinsic muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus) move the tongue in three dimensions for chewing and swallowing.

b: Unilateral palsy → tongue deviates to weak side
Bilateral palsy → central tongue depression, airway obstruction
Common causes: neck trauma, carotid surgery, skull base tumors, tuberculous meningitis
sections.p: Lesions produce ipsilateral tongue weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations. The classic bedside sign is deviation of the tongue toward the side of the lesion when protruded.

t.b: Localises lesion; if unavailable, use CT scan or bedside ultrasound of neck vessels
Confirms denervation; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam

b: No deviation but dysarthria = consider cortical stroke
sections.p: At the bedside, ask the patient to stick out the tongue and observe direction, strength, and presence of fasciculations. Test palate elevation (CN X) to differentiate central from peripheral causes of dysarthria.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive tongue weakness causing drooling and aspiration
Bilateral hypoglossal palsy with airway compromise
Rapidly expanding neck mass with nerve deficit
